title: Sigmoid
Squash Any Number to (0, 1)

intro.before: Sigmoid turns any real number into a value between 0 and 1. That makes it
intro.after: for yes/no predictions, and the gate inside LSTMs.

idea.text: Feed in any score, from −∞ to +∞. Large positive scores land near 1, large negative ones near 0, and a score of exactly 0 lands at 0.5. The curve is smooth, so gradients can flow through it.
points: The output is always strictly between 0 and 1
Its slope peaks at x = 0 and fades in both tails

legend.text: the input score (a logit), any real number
the output, read as a probability
the slope that backprop multiplies by

formula.note: The slope reuses the output, so it costs no extra exponential.

example.title: Worked example
example.tagline: one input, all the way through

figures.title: The S-curve
figures.caption: σ(−2) = 0.12, σ(0) = 0.5, σ(2) = 0.88. Big inputs flatten out near 0 or 1.

figures.title: Why gradients vanish
figures.caption: The slope is at most 0.25, so ten stacked sigmoids shrink a gradient about a millionfold.

items.text: Logistic regression and yes/no output heads

items.name: Multi-label outputs
items.text: One independent sigmoid per label, e.g. tags

items.name: LSTM and GRU gates
items.text: Each gate is a sigmoid: 0 blocks, 1 lets through

items.name: SiLU and GLU layers
items.text: SiLU is x · σ(x); gated layers scale by σ

pros: Reads directly as a probability for yes/no and multi-label tasks
Smooth everywhere, with a slope that costs one multiply: σ(1 − σ)
With binary cross-entropy the gradient is simply ŷ − y
cons: Slope is at most 0.25, so deep stacks of sigmoids vanish gradients
Saturates: at x = 10 the slope is 0.0000454, so learning stalls
Outputs are never centred on 0, which slows hidden-layer training

principles.sub: Hidden layers train faster with ReLU-family activations; keep sigmoid for yes/no heads.
BCEWithLogitsLoss fuses sigmoid and log, which stays stable for big scores.
σ′(5) ≈ 0.0066; normalise inputs so scores stay in the steep middle.

quote.big: Any number in, a probability out.
quote.small: Steep in the middle, flat at the edges.
